question: Why does breadth-first search find shortest paths?

turns.response:
{"topic": "Breadth-First Search finds shortest paths (unweighted graphs)",
 "summary": "In an unweighted graph, BFS explores vertices in nondecreasing order of distance from the source by processing a FIFO queue level by level. The essence: the queue always holds vertices whose distances differ by at most one, so a vertex is first reached along a path of minimum possible length — no shorter path can appear later because everything closer was already dequeued first.",

   {"title": "Rings grow one step at a time", "claim": "All distance-1 vertices are settled before any distance-2 vertex, forming concentric frontier layers."},
   {"title": "The queue never skips a layer", "claim": "The FIFO order guarantees the queue holds only distances d and d+1 at once, so layers finish in order."},
   {"title": "First visit is the shortest", "claim": "Because closer vertices are always dequeued first, the distance assigned on first discovery is minimal and never improves later."},
   {"title": "Trace the tree back home", "claim": "Following parent pointers from any vertex to the source yields a path of exactly its BFS distance — a shortest path."}
